newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish king dragged into political skirmish.
newsitem.headline: Spanish king dragged into political skirmish.

text.p: Spanish King Juan Carlos found himself caught in the crossfire of a political skirmish on Tuesday involving the ruling conservatives, the socialist ex-rulers and the communists.

Battle was joined when Communist Party chief Julio Anguita suggested the king -- revered by the Spaniards for his key role in re-establishing democracy after nearly 40 years of dictatorship -- be replaced by a republican government.
Popular Party (PP) Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar at first dismissed the suggestion as absurd, saying he would not stoop to entering such an argument.

But then former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, entering the political arena after many months of silence, blasted the PP government for creating an atmosphere in which someone could dare to question the cherished post-dictatorship constitution.
This drew a riposte from a source in Aznar's office who called Gonzalez irresponsible and warned the conservatives would fight dirty if needed, according to the state news agency Efe.
"He's started a very dangerous game," the source quoted by Efe said. "But he has to be warned that if he continues down this path the government will also play with the same rules."
Aznar had tried to side-step the debate, which heated up on Monday when Anguita said the king overstepped constitutional bounds with comments on Spain's membership of NATO and the European Union.
When asked if the king should comment on such subjects, Aznar said there was no reason to enter the debate.
"(Anguita) has entered the realm of the absurd," Aznar said. "The immense majority of Spaniards, and I'm among them, won't participate with the criteria that he has placed on the table."

Anguita's outburst followed two weeks of harsh attacks on the government for defying court requests to declassify secret files on a 1980s "dirty war" which the former Socialist government is alleged to have waged against Basque separatists.
The Communists contend that Aznar's conservative government, like the Socialists before it, breached constitutional principles by refusing to hand over the documents.

But Anguita has drawn criticism from politicians of all stripes, even from members of his own United Left (IU) coalition, for suggesting that since the current constitution is being abused it should be changed.
His cry for a pre-Civil War republic was particularly contentious in a nation that holds near-fanatical reverence for the king.
The charismatic and thoughtful Communist leader insists that it is his democratic right to criticise the head of state and other Spanish institutions.
But his willingness to talk about PCE withdrawal from a multi-party pact defending the constitution has torpedoed chances of mounting a credible left-wing alliance in opposition to the PP government.
The PCE is the majority partner of the IU coalition, which controls 21 of parliament's 350 seats and a potential swing vote against the PP if thrown in with the Socialists.
Gonzalez criticised Anguita's message about the republic -- in existence before and during the 1936-39 Civil War -- and said it "seriously complicated" efforts to reach a Socialist-IU understanding.
"Looking for agreements with the political group led by Anguita is complicated when there's not even consensus on the basic elements," Gonzalez told a party congress on Tuesday.
"The Communist Party made an enormous effort to get the constitutional consensus, but Anguita's comments have put his own work in question."
